question.text: This word describes the illegal production and sale of liquor during Prohibition. It also applies to anything taken without permission and distributed for profit.
question.clue: The Purple Gang in Detroit had a major influence on this industry, which imported its main product from Belle Isle and Windsor.

swap.leadin: Answer the following about odd presidential pets.
swap.text: This president owned a pet raccoon named Rebecca. This former Massachusetts governor famously said "You lose" to a woman who tried to win a bet by getting him to say more than two words.
swap.clue: The Bonus Act was passed despite this president's veto.

question.text: Washington was invited by this President, who took office after the death of William McKinley. In his military career, this man fought with the "Buffalo Soldiers" as leader of the Rough Riders.
question.clue: In his greatest office, he directed the Great White Fleet of the U.S. Navy to make a two-year circumnavigation of the globe.

swap.text: Susan B. Anthony fought for this amendment to the Constitution that legally granted women the right to vote.
swap.clue: Specters of a new Force Bill were used by "antis" like Josephine Parker to argue against this legislation on racial grounds.

question.leadin: The plaintiff in this case appealed his violation of the Bakeshop Act of 1895, which stated that bakery employees could only work 60 hours a week.
question.text: Name this progressive-era case, which upheld the "liberty of contract" in ruling against limiting the hours that bakers could work.
question.answerHtml: Lochner v. New York [or New York v. Lochner]
question.clue: This case's decision lost influence with the "switch in time that saved nine" which ruled the government could restrict the liberty of contract in West Coast Hotel v. Parrish.

swap.leadin: Answer the following about Hull House, a settlement house that was a hub of social reform in the early 20th century.
swap.text: This American reformer founded Hull House with Ellen Starr as a "community of university women," who would teach classes to working-class people. She was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 1931.
swap.clue: This first American woman to win a Nobel Peace Prize worked closely with Ellen Gates Starr.

question.leadin: This president once said to a delegation of African-American professionals, "Segregation is not a humiliation but a benefit, and ought to be so regarded by you gentlemen."
question.text: Name this president who also did good things like passing the Clayton Antitrust Act, Federal Reserve Act, and Keating-Owen Act.
question.clue: A group of protesters during his presidency was placed in Occoquan Prison and tortured by W .

swap.leadin: William Boehner was killed by a bomb intended for the namesake of these events.
swap.text: Name these events led by a namesake Attorney General that unlawfully detained thousands of suspected left-wingers and anarchists during the First Red Scare.
swap.clue: Some targets of these events, which were led by a man nicknamed the "Fighting Quaker,"were placed on the ship Buford, nicknamed the "Soviet Ark."

question.leadin: Answer the following about the La Follette family.
question.text: "Fighting Bob" ran for president in 1924 under a short-lived political party of this name. A former president running for a party with this name finished second behind Woodrow Wilson in the 1912 presidential election.
question.clue: Perhaps the greatest electoral successes of a party by this name came earlier, in California, where Hiram Johnson was elected governor and then Senator on its banner.

swap.text: Before becoming executive director, Wilkins spent fifteen years editing this NAACP magazine, previously overseen by W.E.B. DuBois and Jessie Fauset.
swap.clue: It begins by noting that the "summer soldier" and the "sunshine patriot" will shrink from facing the title challenge, in which "these are the times that try men's souls."

question.leadin: Answer the following about goings-on in Warren Gamaliel Harding's administration.
question.text: Harding's only Secretary of State was this man, a former New York governor who resigned the Supreme Court to run for president, lost, then was appointed Chief Justice.
question.clue: He replaced Bainbridge Colby as Secretary of State and chaired the Washington Naval Conference.

swap.leadin: His novel Oil! provided the basis for the film There Will Be Blood.
swap.text: Who was this Socialist author of King Coal and a series of books about Lanny Budd?
swap.clue: He wrote about J. P. Morgan in The Moneychangers and about a Colorado strike in King Coal, and won a Pulitzer Prize for his novel Dragon's Teeth.

question.leadin: Dr. Harvey Wiley's unethical experiments on the volunteer "poison squad" led to the passage of this bill.
question.text: Name this Square Deal act initially enforced by the Bureau of Chemistry. Robert La Follette criticized one industry's "villainous devices" to support this act, which was also supported by a 1906 novel that "hit the public in the stomach."
question.clue: The Supreme Court held that it did not apply to therapeutic claims in United States v. Johnson.

swap.text: Indians who complied with the Dawes Act were granted American citizenship by this act, which was proposed by a New York Republican and signed into law in 1924.

question.text: The Keating-Owen act lost much of its power in this case, in which a North Carolina father sued after his son was prohibited from working in a cotton mill.
question.clue: The opinion was written by William Rufus Day for the Edward White Court, which made this ruling 5-4 as McKenna, Clarke, and Brandeis joined in a dissent written by Holmes.

swap.text: As well as introducing police forces, as Prime Minister, Peel reinstituted this measure in 1842, which had been first introduced by Pitt the Younger. This measure had previously been abolished after the Battle of Waterloo, but would not be abolished again.
swap.clue: Congress first passed a peacetime version of this concept with the Wilson-Gorman tariff.

question.leadin: Answer some questions about labor-movement related strike.
question.text: This man, the fourth governor of Idaho, was assassinated by Harry Orchard in 1905. Big Bill Haywood was heavily investigated in connection with the assassination.
question.clue: This governor of Idaho who was assassinated in 1905 by Harry Orchard.

swap.text: This successor to the Elkins Act extended the Interstate Commerce Committee's power to impose fines and maximum rates to ferries and bridges, among other transportation venues.
swap.clue: Passed in 1906, it gave the ICC the power to regulate interstate railroad rates as it forbade railroads from raising them without approval.

question.text: In opposition to the Treaty of Versailles, Johnson was a member of the Irreconcilables, a faction led by Henry Cabot Lodge and this senator, dubbed the "Lion of Idaho." He prosecuted Big Bill Haywood for the murder of Governor Frank Steunenberg.
question.clue: This Idaho senator was one of the "irreconcilables" who opposed ratification of the Treaty of Versailles. This senator earlier prosecuted Big Bill Haywood.
